673.title: Diwali: the row of lamps
673.hook: Rama comes home after fourteen years, and a whole city lights lamps to show him the way
673.howItsDone: At Diwali, Hindu families clean and decorate their homes, draw rangoli at the door, light rows of clay oil lamps, worship Lakshmi on the new-moon night, share sweets, visit relatives and set off fireworks; many keep all five days.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Navaratri, nine nights of the Goddess, and the tenth day of victory. Your line was nine nights, then the dawn. Did you refuse one small thing for one night? Day six hundred seventy-three.
screen: `NINE NIGHTS, THEN THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: The darkest night of the month. No moon at all. And on that night, a whole city does the opposite of sleeping. Every doorstep, every windowsill, every wall gets a small clay lamp, a little cup of oil with a cotton wick. The story many families tell their children is simple: Rama is coming home after fourteen years, and the people of Ayodhya light the way so he can find it in the dark. We read Valmiki's homecoming earlier. Today, the festival that grew around it.
screen: `NO MOON TONIGHT.` → `A LAMP ON EVERY DOORSTEP.` → `SO HE CAN FIND HIS WAY.`

segments.voice: Diwali is short for Deepavali. Deepa means lamp. Avali means a row, a line. A row of lamps. That's the whole name, and it's an exact description. The main night falls on amavasya, the new moon, in the month of Kartika in many calendars, usually in October or November. So the lamps are lit on purpose on the darkest night of the month. For many families, Diwali is actually five days. It starts with Dhanteras, when people buy something new, often metal, for the home. Then Naraka Chaturdashi, with its own story, which we'll meet another day. Then the main night, when many families worship Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth and good fortune, and leave doors and windows open and lit so she can come in. People draw rangoli, patterns of colored powder or rice flour, at the threshold to welcome her. The fourth day honors Krishna lifting Govardhan hill, and in some regions the king Bali. The fifth, Bhai Dooj, is for brothers and sisters. The reasons given for the lamps vary by region: Rama's return, Lakshmi's visit, Krishna's victory. Diwali's night is shared with neighbors too: Jains mark it as the night Mahavira attained liberation, and Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, a guru's release from prison, on the same night. Different stories, the same small flame. And every one of them asks the lamp to do the same job: make it possible to find the way in.
screen: `DEEPA: LAMP. AVALI: A ROW.` · `THE DARKEST NIGHT OF THE MONTH.` · `FIVE DAYS, AND LAKSHMI AT THE DOOR.` · `MANY STORIES, ONE FLAME.` · then, large: `LIGHT THE WAY HOME.`

segments.voice: If it's safe and you have one, light a candle, or switch on one small lamp, and turn off the others. Look at the light for a few breaths. Then think of someone who's far from home right now, in distance or in some other way. Picture this light set in a window for them. You don't need words. Just hold the light and the person together, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Diwali. Deepavali, a row of lamps, lit on the new-moon night for Rama's return, for Lakshmi's visit, and for more stories besides.
screen: `DIWALI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: light the way home. Today, leave one light on for someone, a message, a porch light, a seat saved, so they know where to find you. Day six hundred seventy-three.

screen: `DAY 673 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HOLI: THE FESTIVAL OF COLORS.`

674.title: Holi: the festival of colors
674.hook: Prahlad walks out of the fire unharmed; the next morning everyone throws color and nobody is a stranger
674.tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
674.howItsDone: On the full-moon night of Phalguna, many Hindus light the Holika Dahan bonfire and circle it with offerings; the next morning they play with colored powder and water, visit friends and family, and share sweets like gujiya.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Diwali, the row of lamps on the darkest night. Your line was light the way home. Did you leave a light on for someone? Today, a fire the night before, and color the morning after. Day six hundred seventy-four.
screen: `LIGHT THE WAY HOME.`

segments.voice: In the days before Holi, in many villages and city lanes, a pile starts to grow at a crossroads or an open patch of ground: branches, scrap wood, cakes of dried cow dung, whatever people can spare. Sometimes a small figure is set on top. On the full-moon night, people gather around it at dusk. They walk around it, offer grain and coconut, and then they light it. Tomorrow these streets will be pink and green. Tonight belongs to the fire, and the fire has a name.
screen: `A PILE GROWS AT THE CROSSROADS.` → `LIT ON THE FULL-MOON NIGHT.` → `THE FIRE HAS A NAME.`

segments.voice: The bonfire is called Holika Dahan, the burning of Holika. The story behind it belongs to a demon king, Hiranyakashipu, who has made himself almost impossible to kill and demands to be worshiped. His own son, Prahlad, a boy, won't do it. Prahlad is devoted to Vishnu, and says so. The Bhagavata Purana tells how the king tried again and again to destroy his son, and how every attempt failed. The version Holi remembers adds the king's sister, Holika. In the story people tell, Holika could not be harmed by fire, and she sits in a blazing pyre with the boy in her lap, to burn him. Instead, the fire takes her, and Prahlad walks out unharmed, still saying the name of Vishnu. So the bonfire is a remembering: the cruelty burned, the trusting child safe. Then comes the morning. The day after the full moon of Phalguna, at the edge of spring, the streets fill with gulal, colored powder, and water. And for that one morning, the usual lines blur. Neighbors who don't speak, bosses and workers, old and young, all get the same handful of pink on the face. Nobody can tell who anyone is, and that's partly the point. Many people use Holi to visit, forgive, and start again. The story is about a boy who wouldn't bow to a tyrant. The festival turns it into a morning when nobody stands above anybody else.
screen: `HOLIKA DAHAN: THE BONFIRE.` · `PRAHLAD WON'T BOW.` · `THE FIRE TAKES HOLIKA, NOT THE BOY.` · `GULAL: THE SAME COLOR ON EVERYONE.` · then, large: `EVERYONE'S THE SAME COLOR TODAY.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Bring to mind one small grudge, not the biggest one, just a small one you've been carrying: someone who didn't reply, a remark that stung. Picture it as a stick of wood. On an out-breath, lay it on a fire and watch it catch. You don't have to forgive the person yet. Just set down the stick, and feel your hands empty. The bell holds the time.
Holi. A bonfire for Prahlad's rescue from the fire, then a spring morning of color when everyone looks the same.
screen: `HOLI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: everyone's the same color today. Today, treat one person you'd normally rank above or below you as just exactly level with you. Day six hundred seventy-four.

screen: `DAY 674 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: MAHA SHIVARATRI: THE GREAT NIGHT OF SHIVA.`

675.title: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
675.hook: a night kept awake, water poured over the lingam, Om Namah Shivaya until dawn
675.tomorrow: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
675.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus fast, visit Shiva temples, pour water or milk over the lingam with bilva leaves, and keep vigil through the night repeating Om Namah Shivaya; many temples stay open until dawn.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Holi, a bonfire for Prahlad and a morning of color. Your line was everyone's the same color today. Did you treat someone as exactly level with you? Today, a night nobody sleeps. Day six hundred seventy-five.
screen: `EVERYONE'S THE SAME COLOR TODAY.`

segments.voice: A hunter goes into the forest and finds nothing. All day, nothing. Night falls, and he's too far from home and too stubborn to go back empty-handed. So he climbs a tree beside a pool, where animals will come to drink, and he waits. He hasn't eaten. He can't let himself sleep, or he'll fall. To keep busy, he plucks leaves off the branch, one by one, and drops them. He doesn't look where they land. This is one of the stories told on Maha Shivaratri, and it's about a man who keeps the festival perfectly without knowing it exists.
screen: `A HUNTER WITH NOTHING.` → `A TREE BESIDE A POOL.` → `LEAVES DROPPED IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Shiva-ratri: the night of Shiva. Maha: great. It falls on the fourteenth night of the waning moon, in late winter, the last dark before the new moon. The tree the hunter climbed was a bilva tree, whose three-part leaves are sacred to Shiva. And under it, hidden in the dark, was a lingam, the simple rounded stone that stands for Shiva in temples and shrines. All night, his dropped leaves fell on it. Drops from his water pot spilled on it. He fasted, because he had no food. He stayed awake, because he had to. Without meaning to, he had done what Shivaratri asks: fast, keep vigil, offer water and bilva leaves to the lingam. In the Shiva Purana's telling, deer come to the pool through the night, and each one asks to be spared long enough to go home first, and the hunter, softening, lets them go. By dawn, the story says, his heart is changed, and Shiva's grace reaches him. That's what people across India do on this night, on purpose. Temples stay open until morning. Devotees pour water, milk, honey over the lingam, in a rite called abhisheka. Many repeat five syllables, na-mah shi-va-ya, Om Namah Shivaya, bowing to Shiva, over and over until the sky gets light. Different stories are given for the night: Shiva's marriage to Parvati, or the night he drank the world's poison. But the practice is the same: don't sleep through the night that matters.
screen: `MAHA SHIVARATRI: THE GREAT NIGHT.` · `BILVA LEAVES FALL ON A HIDDEN LINGAM.` · `A FAST AND A VIGIL, BY ACCIDENT.` · `OM NAMAH SHIVAYA UNTIL DAWN.` · then, large: `STAY AWAKE FOR WHAT MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Sit upright, the way the hunter had to stay upright on his branch. Follow your breath in and out. When you feel the first urge to stop, to check your phone, to shift, to be done, stay for three more breaths. Just three. Count them gently. Then notice what's here on the other side of that urge. Keep going with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Shivaratri. The night of Shiva, kept awake with fasting, water and bilva leaves on the lingam, and Om Namah Shivaya until dawn.
screen: `SHIVARATRI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: stay awake for what matters. Today, give one thing you'd normally half-attend, a conversation, a meal, a walk, your full waking attention. Day six hundred seventy-five.

676.title: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
676.hook: a sister ties a thread on her brother's wrist, and he promises to look after her
676.carry: a thread can hold a promise
676.tomorrow: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born
676.howItsDone: On the full moon of Shravana, sisters perform a short aarti for their brothers, mark their foreheads, tie a rakhi on the right wrist and feed them a sweet; brothers give a gift and a promise of protection. Many families now include cousins, friends and sisters tying rakhis on sisters.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shivaratri, the night of Shiva, and a hunter who kept it by accident. Your line was stay awake for what matters. What got your full attention? Day six hundred seventy-six.
screen: `STAY AWAKE FOR WHAT MATTERS.`

segments.voice: In August, in office lifts and school corridors across India, you'll notice something on boys' and men's wrists: bright threads, some plain red and gold, some with a big foam flower or a cartoon character on them. Some men have six or seven, up to the elbow. Each one was tied by a sister, or a cousin, or a friend who calls him brother. Ask him to take one off and he'll look at you like you asked him to throw away a letter.
screen: `THREADS ON EVERY WRIST.` → `SOME UP TO THE ELBOW.` → `EACH ONE TIED BY A SISTER.`

segments.voice: Raksha means protection. Bandhan means a tie, a binding. Raksha Bandhan: the tie of protection. The thread itself is the rakhi. The festival falls on the full moon of the month of Shravana, in the monsoon. The ritual is short, and in many Hindu homes it looks like this. The sister prepares a small plate: a lamp, a little red powder, a few grains of rice, sweets, the rakhi. She puts a mark on her brother's forehead, waves the lamp before him, and ties the thread on his right wrist. She feeds him a sweet. He gives her a gift, and a promise: to look after her, to stand by her. That's all. A thread costs almost nothing. What makes it heavy is what's tied into it. There are several stories behind the thread. One, often told, is that Draupadi tore a strip from her sari to bind Krishna's bleeding finger, and Krishna promised to protect her; in that telling, he keeps the promise when she is humiliated at the dice game. That story is widely loved, though the episode of the torn sari isn't found in the Mahabharata's text itself; it comes from the telling. In Puranic tradition, a protective thread is tied for the god Indra before a battle. We'll meet that one another day. Today, the festival has stretched. Sisters tie rakhis on sisters. Friends tie them on friends. And people send them across oceans in envelopes, so that a promise made in one city gets worn on a wrist in another.
screen: `RAKSHA: PROTECTION. BANDHAN: A TIE.` · `A MARK, A LAMP, A THREAD, A SWEET.` · `DRAUPADI'S TORN SARI, AS IT'S TOLD.` · `RAKHIS MAILED ACROSS OCEANS.` · then, large: `A THREAD CAN HOLD A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and rest your left hand around your right wrist, lightly, where a rakhi would go. Feel your pulse, or just the warmth. Now bring to mind one person you'd protect if you had to: a sibling, a friend, a child, a neighbor. Hold them in mind while you hold your wrist. Let the promise form without words. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Rakhi. The thread tied on Raksha Bandhan, the tie of protection: a sister's thread, and a brother's promise to look after her.
screen: `RAKHI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a thread can hold a promise. Today, tell the person you thought of that you're there for them, in a message or out loud. Day six hundred seventy-six.

screen: `DAY 676 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: JANMASHTAMI: THE NIGHT KRISHNA WAS BORN.`

677.title: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born
677.hook: a prison at midnight, a river that parts, and a baby carried across it to safety
677.howItsDone: Many Hindus fast on Janmashtami, sing bhajans and read the birth story, bathe and dress an image of baby Krishna at midnight and rock it in a cradle, then break the fast with milk sweets; in Maharashtra, Dahi Handi teams build human pyramids the next day.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: rakhi, a thread tied on a brother's wrist, and a promise of protection. Your line was a thread can hold a promise. Did you tell someone you're there for them? Day six hundred seventy-seven.
screen: `A THREAD CAN HOLD A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: A week ago we stood in Kamsa's prison at midnight and watched Vasudeva carry his son across the Yamuna. Today, the same night, from the other side: the kitchen. Because for many Hindu families, Janmashtami isn't only a story told. It's a day cooked, sung and stayed up for. And the morning after, in Maharashtra, young men climb on each other's shoulders, level on level, to reach a clay pot of yogurt hanging over the street.
screen: `THE SAME NIGHT, FROM THE KITCHEN.` → `A DAY COOKED, SUNG, STAYED UP FOR.` → `A HUMAN TOWER AND A POT.`

segments.voice: The day begins with a fast. Some take no food at all, some only fruit and milk, until midnight. In the evening, the shrine is decorated, and a small cradle, a jhula, is set up for the baby Krishna, sometimes on a swing. People sing bhajans, devotional songs, and in many homes read the birth story from the Bhagavata. As midnight comes, everyone gathers. At twelve, the conch sounds, the image of baby Krishna is bathed in milk and yogurt and honey, dressed in tiny new clothes, and rocked in the cradle. Only then is the fast broken, often with sweets made of milk and butter. Why butter? Because the baby carried across the river grows up in Gokul, among cowherds, and the Bhagavata tells how he and his friends raid the neighbors' houses for butter and yogurt. The women of the village come to his mother, Yashoda, to complain: he steals our butter, he feeds it to the monkeys, he breaks the pots. The women hang the pots high, out of reach; he piles up stools and mortars and climbs to get them. Devotees call him Makhan Chor, the butter thief, with deep affection. That's the root of Dahi Handi, the yogurt pot. The day after Janmashtami, teams called govindas form human pyramids in the street to break a pot hung high above them, while crowds cheer. So Janmashtami holds both: the solemn midnight when the good arrives, and the cheerful chaos of the child it arrives as.

678.title: Ganesh Chaturthi: welcoming Ganesha home
678.hook: clay Ganeshas are carried home with drums, kept for days, then given back to the water
678.carry: welcome it, then let it go
678.tomorrow: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
678.howItsDone: Some Hindu families avoid looking at the moon on the night of Ganesh Chaturthi, and some read or hear the Syamantaka jewel story as a remedy if they see it by accident.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Janmashtami from the kitchen, a cradle at midnight and a tower for a pot of yogurt. Your line was the good arrives at midnight. Did you prepare something for someone? Day six hundred seventy-eight.
screen: `THE GOOD ARRIVES AT MIDNIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's a strange rule some families keep on Ganesh Chaturthi. With a clay Ganesha just carried home, drums still echoing in the street, a grandmother says: whatever you do tonight, don't look at the moon. Kids who've never heard it before immediately want to look. Why would anyone be told not to look at the moon on Ganesha's own birthday? Because, people say, Ganesha and the moon once had a very bad evening.
screen: `A CLAY GUEST, JUST ARRIVED.` → `DON'T LOOK AT THE MOON TONIGHT.` → `A VERY BAD EVENING.`

segments.voice: The story, as it's told, goes like this. On his birthday, Ganesha has been offered modak after modak, the sweet dumplings, and he's eaten them all. Late at night, very full, he's riding home on his mouse. A snake crosses the path. The mouse panics, Ganesha tumbles off, and his belly splits, modaks rolling everywhere. In some tellings he ties his belly back up with the snake. And up in the sky, the moon, proud of his beauty, laughs at him. Ganesha, embarrassed and furious, curses the moon: whoever looks at you will be falsely accused. The moon is horrified. The gods come to plead. And here's the part worth noticing. Ganesha softens. He doesn't take the curse back completely, but he narrows it: it will hold only on this one night, the fourth day of his month. That's why some families keep their eyes down on Chaturthi night. Tradition even names someone it happened to. In some tellings, Krishna glimpses the moon on Chaturthi and is soon accused of stealing a famous jewel, the Syamantaka. The Bhagavata Purana tells the jewel story, how Krishna was suspected and had to go and find the jewel to clear his name; the link to the moon comes from other tellings. People say that hearing the jewel story lifts the curse if you looked by accident. Underneath the comedy is a small teaching about anger. Ganesha's embarrassment was real. He didn't pretend it wasn't. But he let most of it go.

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Recall a recent moment when someone laughed at you, or you felt foolish. Let yourself feel it again, just a little: the heat in the face, the urge to snap back. Hold it, the way you'd hold something heavy in both hands. Then, on a slow out-breath, set it down. Not all of it, maybe. Just most of it. Rest with what's left. The bell holds the time.
Ganesh Chaturthi. Ganesha's fourth day, and the night, people say, not to look at the moon, after the god who softened his own curse.

679.title: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
679.hook: Durga meets the buffalo demon; nine nights of dancing, and on the tenth day the good wins
679.howItsDone: Many Hindus honor one of the nine forms of Durga, the Navadurga, on each night of Navaratri, with that form's prayers and offerings; some fast all nine days, some wear a set color each day, and many end by honoring young girls as the Goddess on the eighth or ninth day.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ganesh Chaturthi, and the night not to look at the moon. Your line was welcome it, then let it go. Did you let most of an embarrassment go? Day six hundred seventy-nine.
screen: `WELCOME IT, THEN LET IT GO.`

segments.voice: Walk into a Hindu home in North India during Navaratri and you may find a small calendar taped near the shrine, one name for each night. Night one has one name, night two another, all the way to nine. Some families wear a different color each day to match. It looks like nine goddesses. Ask the grandmother who keeps the calendar, and she'll likely tell you: it's one Goddess, nine ways. Last week we watched her defeat the buffalo demon. Today, her nine faces.
screen: `A CALENDAR BY THE SHRINE.` → `ONE NAME FOR EACH NIGHT.` → `ONE GODDESS, NINE WAYS.`

segments.voice: The nine forms are called the Navadurga, nine Durgas. In the most common list, they move through a life. First Shailaputri, daughter of the mountain: Parvati, born to the Himalaya. Second, Brahmacharini, the one who practices austerity, Parvati in the forest fasting and meditating to win Shiva. Then Chandraghanta, with a crescent moon like a bell on her brow, fierce and protective. Kushmanda, who in tradition smiled the universe into being. Skandamata, the mother of Skanda, her son. Katyayani, the warrior who faces Mahisha. Kalaratri, the dark night, the most terrifying form, who destroys fear itself. Mahagauri, radiant white, calm again. And Siddhidatri, the giver of every attainment. Look at the arc: a daughter, a seeker, a protector, a creator, a mother, a warrior, a darkness, a peace, a fullness. Devotees honor one each night, with that form's prayers and offerings. Some fast all nine days; others on the first and last. The second night's story has a turning point worth knowing. Parvati loves Shiva, but he's lost in meditation and wants nothing. Rather than give up, she goes into the forest and practices austerity so fierce that the sages are astonished, until Shiva comes to her himself. That's Brahmacharini. And this week has carried its own row of forms: lamps on the darkest night, colors after a fire, a vigil for Shiva, a thread on a wrist, a cradle at midnight, a moon not to look at, and now nine faces of one Goddess.
screen: `NAVADURGA: NINE FORMS.` · `DAUGHTER, SEEKER, PROTECTOR, CREATOR.` · `MOTHER, WARRIOR, DARK NIGHT, PEACE.` · `BRAHMACHARINI: SHE DOESN'T GIVE UP.` · then, large: `ONE GODDESS, NINE WAYS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and breathe. Think of the different people you've been this week: someone's child, someone's friend, a worker, a worrier, someone who laughed, someone who was tired. Let each one come up for a breath, and greet it. Then let them all settle into the one person breathing right now: many faces, one you. The bell holds the time.
Navaratri. Nine nights, and in many homes one form of the Goddess for each: the Navadurga, from mountain daughter to giver of every attainment.
screen: `NAVARATRI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: nine nights, then the dawn. Tonight, keep going at one thing you've wanted to give up on, the way Brahmacharini did. Day six hundred seventy-nine.
